approachQuestion.prompt:
Dispatch list

Each record is (id, urgency, arrival). Return all IDs ordered by higher urgency first, then smaller arrival first, then smaller ID first. IDs are distinct integers; urgency and arrival can tie. Input order carries no priority. Do not change the input records.

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 200,000; all fields are integers from 0 to 1,000,000,000; each comparison is constant-time.

Examples: [(9,3,7),(2,3,7),(4,5,9)] → [4,2,9]. [(6,1,8),(3,1,2)] → [3,6].

Choose the most efficient valid method among these options under the stated model; avoid removable repeated work.
constraints: The complete input/output and mutation contract in the prompt applies to every option.

options.text: Sort a copy of the records using urgency descending, arrival ascending, and ID ascending as a single lexicographic comparator, then emit IDs.
options.feedback: The comparator encodes every priority level, including the final tie, and copying preserves the input.

options.text: Stably sort a copy by urgency descending only, then emit IDs.
options.feedback: Stability preserves input order, not the required tie order: [(9,3,7),(2,3,7)] would emit [9,2] instead of [2,9].

options.text: Sort a copy by urgency ascending, arrival ascending, and ID ascending.
options.feedback: The primary direction is reversed: [(6,1,8),(4,5,9)] must put ID 4 first.

options.text: Copy records; repeatedly scan all remaining records for the next record using the full priority rule, emit its ID and remove it.
options.feedback: All priorities are respected, but repeated full scans add avoidable work compared with sorting once.

feedback.reason: Apply every comparator field in the stated order.
details: Use comparison merge sort on a copied record array with the full lexicographic comparator; emit IDs in that order.
Apply every comparator field in the stated order. A secondary field matters only when all preceding fields tie; sorting by one field alone can misorder otherwise equal-primary records.

“Sort a copy of the records using urgency descending, arrival ascending, and ID ascending as a single lexicographic comparator, then emit IDs.”: The comparator encodes every priority level, including the final tie, and copying preserves the input.
“Stably sort a copy by urgency descending only, then emit IDs.”: Stability preserves input order, not the required tie order: [(9,3,7),(2,3,7)] would emit [9,2] instead of [2,9].
“Sort a copy by urgency ascending, arrival ascending, and ID ascending.”: The primary direction is reversed: [(6,1,8),(4,5,9)] must put ID 4 first.

“Copy records; repeatedly scan all remaining records for the next record using the full priority rule, emit its ID and remove it.”: All priorities are respected, but repeated full scans add avoidable work compared with sorting once.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed method using conventional comparison merge sort with a linear merge buffer and a logarithmic recursion stack. Choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space bounds in n. Count all working copies, indexed records, buffers and stack frames; exclude the caller input and returned output. No hashing is used. Comparisons, arithmetic, record copies and array accesses take constant time; preallocate output capacity so no resizing assumption is needed.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(n) additional space
O(n log n) time, O(1) additional space

feedback.reason: Sort the copied records, then emit IDs in one pass.
details: Sorting dominates the linear scan: O(n log n) worst-case time. The merge buffer and copied/indexed records use O(n) auxiliary memory; the O(log n) recursion stack does not change this total. The output is excluded. The quadratic-time option overstates the tight bound, constant space omits the buffer, and linear time omits comparison sorting.
